sections.skill: Recognize common informal fallacies in self-contained arguments

questions.prompt: Definitions: Attacking the person: rejecting a claim because of who made it, instead of because of the reasons given. Hasty generalization: drawing a broad conclusion from too few cases. Circular reasoning: using the conclusion, in other words, as a reason for itself. Appeal to popularity: claiming something is true because many people believe it. Dana argues that the library should stay open later. Raj replies: "Dana is always late to class, so her opinion about library hours does not count." Which fallacy is this?

Definitions: False choice: presenting only two options when others are possible. Slippery slope: claiming, without support, that one step will lead to a chain of extreme results. Straw man: attacking a distorted version of someone's argument instead of the real one. After, so because: concluding that A caused B only because B happened after A. "Either we cancel the field trip, or every student will get lost in the city." Which fallacy is this?

Definitions: Hasty generalization: drawing a broad conclusion from too few cases. Attacking the person: rejecting a claim because of who made it, instead of because of the reasons given. False choice: presenting only two options when others are possible. Circular reasoning: using the conclusion, in other words, as a reason for itself. "I met two rude people from that town, so everyone from that town is rude." Which fallacy is this?
Definitions: Circular reasoning: using the conclusion, in other words, as a reason for itself. "This app is the best because it is better than all the others" is an example of circular reasoning.

Definitions: After, so because: concluding that A caused B only because B happened after A. Hasty generalization: drawing a broad conclusion from too few cases. Appeal to popularity: claiming something is true because many people believe it. Slippery slope: claiming, without support, that one step will lead to a chain of extreme results. "After I started wearing my lucky socks, our team won three games in a row. The socks made us win." Which fallacy is this?

sections.skill: Strategy: name what the argument does instead of giving reasons
sections.relationship: Students sense that an argument is weak but cannot say why. Asking what the argument does in place of giving real reasons leads to the fallacy's name.
sections.author_note: Students sense that an argument is weak but cannot say why. Asking what the argument does in place of giving real reasons leads to the fallacy's name.

lesson.title: Name what the argument does instead of giving reasons
text: Find the conclusion. Then find what is offered as the reason.
Ask: is the reason about the claim, or about something else (the person, how popular it is, what came first)?
Match what the argument does to a definition: attacking the person, false choice, hasty generalization, circular reasoning, after-so-because, slippery slope, appeal to popularity, straw man.

example.title: Worked example (a different argument)
prompt: "Everyone in my class uses this calculator, so it must give correct answers."
steps: Conclusion: the calculator gives correct answers. Reason: everyone uses it.
The reason is about popularity, not about accuracy: appeal to popularity.

questions.prompt: Definitions: Appeal to popularity: claiming something is true because many people believe it. Straw man: attacking a distorted version of someone's argument instead of the real one. False choice: presenting only two options when others are possible. Slippery slope: claiming, without support, that one step will lead to a chain of extreme results. Which definition describes "Millions of people watch this show, so it must be educational"?
Definitions: Hasty generalization: drawing a broad conclusion from too few cases. Concluding that all dogs are friendly after meeting three friendly dogs is a hasty generalization.

Definitions: Attacking the person: rejecting a claim because of who made it, instead of because of the reasons given. Saying "The bridge design is unsafe because the beams are too thin for the load" is attacking the person.
An argument's reason is about who made a claim rather than about the claim. Which question best helps you notice this?

choices.text: Is the reason about the claim, or about something else?
Do I agree with the conclusion?

questions.correct_answer: Is the reason about the claim, or about something else?

Definitions: Appeal to popularity: claiming something is true because many people believe it. "Most dentists in a large survey recommend brushing twice a day, so brushing twice a day is likely a good idea" is an appeal to popularity.

sections.relationship: Expert: tell fallacies from reasonable arguments.
sections.label: EXPERT CHALLENGE

questions.prompt: Definitions: Attacking the person: rejecting a claim because of who made it, instead of because of the reasons given. Which reply is NOT attacking the person?

choices.text: "Your numbers are from 2010, and the prices have changed since then."
"You are too young to understand prices."
"You only say that because you work for the store."

questions.correct_answer: "Your numbers are from 2010, and the prices have changed since then."

questions.prompt: Definitions: False choice: presenting only two options when others are possible. "A whole number is either even or odd" is a false choice.

Definitions: Hasty generalization: drawing a broad conclusion from too few cases. After, so because: concluding that A caused B only because B happened after A. Straw man: attacking a distorted version of someone's argument instead of the real one. Appeal to popularity: claiming something is true because many people believe it. Which argument avoids all four fallacies defined above?

choices.text: My two cousins liked the plan, so most voters like it.
Everyone online says the plan is good, so it is good.
Our team won after the coach changed shoes, so the shoes helped.
A random sample of 500 voters favored the plan, so most voters probably favor it.

questions.correct_answer: A random sample of 500 voters favored the plan, so most voters probably favor it.

questions.prompt: Definitions: Straw man: attacking a distorted version of someone's argument instead of the real one. Slippery slope: claiming, without support, that one step will lead to a chain of extreme results. Appeal to popularity: claiming something is true because many people believe it. Circular reasoning: using the conclusion, in other words, as a reason for itself. Mo says homework should be shorter on weekends. Lee replies: "So you think students should never study at all? That would be terrible." Which fallacy is this?

Definitions: Slippery slope: claiming, without support, that one step will lead to a chain of extreme results. An argument that predicts a chain of results is always a slippery slope, even when each step is supported by evidence.
